reason: Attacked hardest on the page, because the evidence phrases it loosely as read in place between the printed page numbers 57 and 58, which could mean either page. It holds, and it is 58. I downloaded the OCR of archive.org item al-kindis-metaphysics. Its title page reads A Translation of Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Kindi's Treatise ON FIRST PHILOSOPHY, with Introduction and Commentary by Alfred L. Ivry, State University of New York Press, Albany, 1974, and the copyright page gives 1974 State University of New York; the archive catalogue date of 1990 is metadata noise, not the book. The sentence prints exactly as proposed, apart from Ivry's slash marking the Arabic line break: We ought not to be ashamed of appreciating the truth and of acquiring it wherever it comes from, even if it comes from races distant and nations different from us. On the page, the number sits as a footer beneath each page's text and the running head opens the next, verso reading AL-KINDI'S METAPHYSICS and recto ON FIRST PHILOSOPHY. The sentence falls after the footer 57 and after the verso head AL-KINDI'S METAPHYSICS, and before the footer 58. So it is on page 58, as the source says. Attribution checked with care, since this is the likeliest trap here: the paragraph immediately above quotes Aristotle on being grateful to the fathers of those who have contributed any truth and closes How beautiful is that which he said in this matter, and only then does al-Kindi speak in his own voice. The proposed sentence is al-Kindi's, not the reported Aristotle, so the card's byline is right and no speaker needs naming. shipped.js returns no exact match, no near match, al-kindi at 0 for the year, not banned. Scope: philosophy of the ninth century in a 1974 translation, no scripture, no oratory, nothing needing a warning. Form checks: the source line is 66 characters, leads with the name, and its only dash is the hyphen inside Al-Kindi, not an em dash; the quotation ends in a full stop with no straight double quote; the tag Philosophy is the form of the work; the translator and year of the published translation are named as the rule requires. Two flags for the editor, neither a refutation: the note is empty, and a line saying the sentence is al-Kindi's own and not the Aristotle he has just quoted would earn its place; and this line and 06-phil-09 are both about not shrinking from the search for truth, so the month may not want them on adjacent mornings.
